utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just, with your leave, a couple of points. I'm still hoping to be able to establish a final position on the positioning of Gegaj and Kamenica, but I haven't yet been able to resolve it this morning. If I resolve it before the witness goes, I'll let you know. In fact, Gegaj is shown in Exhibit 83, but not Kamenica. It's on page 9 at D-20. The only other thing I draw to your attention is this: At an earlier stage in the re-examination of this witness there was reference to the Rules of Service. We've checked. They have not been produced in evidence. We have, however, located them, quite a voluminous document, and having a copy printed in both English and B/C/S of those Rules of Service in case they are of any value to the parties or to the Court. I've already made my position on their legality and constitutionality clear in cross-examination, but the document themselves will be available and may perhaps be considered by a later witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's for you to re-examine on these matters if you wish.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly. Certainly, Mr. Robinson. I'll take it in the order in which Mr. Nice asked his questions and put them to General Delic, and I just have several questions, in fact.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Further re-examination by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, a number of witnesses before you and you yesterday were asked by Mr. Nice a question linked to the 30th Personnel Centre. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, at my request, I received from Mr. Nice a document which was sent by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Serbia and Montenegro, and in that document we have annex number 4. That is the document I received yesterday. And I'd now like you to quote just a few portions marked in yellow from that document. So could the document either be placed on the ELMO, on the overhead projector, for General Delic to be able to read what it says in the highlighted portions, although it would be a good idea if he were to read it all, but to save time, the yellow portions will suffice. I'm afraid I don't have a copy in my hands any more, but I would like to ask General Delic to give us the number on the page he's reading from, the ERN number. Otherwise, it has been translated.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 03651994 is the number, the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, would you read out the highlighted portions, please.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In the area of the former Yugoslav Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were about 1.800 persons serving there who, from the time JNA dislocated from Bosnia-Herzegovina, had citizenship of the former Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and who were born on that territory, so that pursuant to a decision on dislocation, they had to stay in that area because the condition to move over to the FRY was the possibility of gaining citizenship of the Republic of Serbia or the Republic of Montenegro, which would be a precondition for joining up with the newly created army of Yugoslavia." Second paragraph: "However, on this occasion there was a great problem of livelihood for the former members of the JNA who had to stay on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The largest number of families of these individuals, because of the war and the fighting on the territory of the former Yugoslavia who came under the rule of the Muslims and Croats found safety and refuge in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as refugees. In the meantime, there were certain -- they had conditions for accommodation and their children started going to school in new schools." "In view of the fact that these individuals were not able to retain their membership as members of the Yugoslav army and that with a situation of this kind they found themselves in a situation which they could not get out of, a solution was found to set up a separate organisational unit, Military Post 3001 Belgrade, that is to say the 30th Personnel Centre in which person -- exclusively persons who had been members of the army of Republika Srpska worked." Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know quite the basis for this re-examination. I'm not going to stand in its way if the Chamber thinks it's helpful, but the Chamber will remember that this is a document that the witness knew nothing about yesterday. I asked him simply whether he knew that a response to an RFA, a request for assistance, about the 30th Personnel Centre had been prepared by the commission. I suggested that it inevitably had been. He didn't accept that. Of course, I didn't advance one second that this was a reliable document; the reverse. So what the -- what the witness is simply being asked to read out is a document provided in answer to an RFA of which he said he knows nothing. But it's up to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Nice is saying that the question doesn't arise out of his further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the contrary, it certainly does arise from that, because you will remember full well, I assume, that yesterday Mr. Nice asked a series of questions about the 30th Personnel Centre and that the witness gave answers in principle but without having a concrete text. So I'm showing him this concrete document from the Foreign Ministry in order to be able to ask him whether that is what he was saying in his responses yesterday without having the grounds for doing so on the basis of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't understand the objection. Plainly the aim of referring to this document was to find out if it explained the 30th Personnel Centre, and here we have the passage which purports to explain it. It's perfectly legitimate re-examination, as far as I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you go on, please, the beginning of the next page.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The basic and sole task of the 30th Personnel Centre was the administrative preparation of documents regulating the material position of the families of the above-mentioned individuals as well as their social welfare insurance, and health insurance. Although this Personnel Centre had its headquarters attached to the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia, it was not within the organisational composition of the army of Yugoslavia but made up a separate, independent organisational entity. In the centre were exclusively members of the army of Republika Srpska worked who during -- in their work used data and records that the personnel department -- administration of the General Staff disposed of for all former members of the JNA. The basis of the authority and competence of the 30th Personnel Centre was as follows: To keep reports of all professional soldiers, officers, non-commissioned officers in permanent service by contract and not on the basis of contracts who from the former JNA remained within the composition of the army of Republika Srpska and were previously serving in the garrisons of the JNA on the territory of that republic," and none of the rest has been highlighted.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters have a copy in English placed on the ELMO, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Keeping records of professional soldiers and civilians working in the former JNA who originated from the former Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and were doing their service in other republics of the SFRY, keeping records of military personnel born on the territory of the former Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, records about the members -- family members of former JNA members born in BH and with residence in the former Yugoslavia, and administrative work with respect to material and social welfare of these individuals and health insurance and other questions of livelihood for the families of the former members of the JNA."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the interpreter asked for a copy in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The copy in English was attached to the document. It was the first document. Might we have a reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They do have them in yesterday's pile of papers, I understand, but it may be not very easy to track them down. The way they'll be able to find them, I think, is that it's attached -- it's attached to the response of -- dated the 21st of November, 2003. So it's underneath a letter that is dated the 21st of November, 2003, the liaison officer of the ICTY, Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I hope that assists the interpreter in finding the document. Mr. Milosevic, I think it is time to -- for you to put a question now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more paragraph at the end, which was highlighted in yellow, and I've just seen it on the ELMO. Might General Delic be allowed to read that, too, for all of us to see?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: One more paragraph, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "It is important to mention that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia nor the army of Yugoslavia on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina after May 1992 had any military formations nor did it in any way take part in the combat on that area -- in that area."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, what it says here in this document, does that coincide with your knowledge about the 30th Personnel Centre in a general nature?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I answered generally speaking yesterday, the centre did exist for the status of individuals to be solved, questions related to their status, whether they originated from the territory of Serbia and lived over there or whether they originated on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because the continuity of the Yugoslav People's Army was transferred to the army of Yugoslavia, and all these personnel documents and files were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, do you happen to know, in view of the fact that we have explained here about the personnel files, health insurance, social insurance, and all the benefits, do you know whether the army of Yugoslavia, the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia or any other organ of Yugoslavia, or Serbia or Montenegro for that matter, ever issued any kind of order to the army of Republika Srpska and could it indeed issue orders? Did it have authority to issue orders to the army of Republika Srpska at all?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. And the army of Republika Srpska, let me say, was a separate army. I don't think anybody from Serbia could issue orders in view of the fact that that other army had its own organisation, establishment, and its chief of the General Staff and Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. That will be sufficient with respect to that particular document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, gentlemen, I should like to mention that Mr. Nice knows full well what the 30th Personnel Centre was because he received this piece of information in 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we don't need comments at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just let us take a look at a few other matters. In yesterday's set of documents provided by Mr. Nice, in tab 3, as far as I can see, yesterday you were shown a document which relates to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may have been in closed session yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't in closed session, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you referring to Rules of Procedure?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. "Rules of Procedure pertaining to the Commission's work of the General Staff of Yugoslavia and Federal Ministry of Defence relating to cooperation with the Hague Tribunal." I don't think we discussed that in closed session yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it was in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, on page -- on page 7, there's a chapter relating to legal assistance, "Providing Legal Aid" is the title. Do you know if this committee ever provided me with any legal aid at all?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it did not. However, I sought legal aid from this commission, or committee, whenever I had any contacts with the investigators. For instance, I asked to be accompanied by a legal advisor working in that commission. Usually I was accompanied by General Bojovic [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, take a look at tab 1, please, which was not a protected document in any way, and would you read out the preamble.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you say Gojovic or Bojovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gojovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. The transcript is wrong. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just the preamble of tab 1. It's just three lines long.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "For the timely assurance of the necessary conditions for performing certain obligations of the Federal Defence Ministry and the General Staff of the army which emanate from the establishment of cooperation between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Hague Tribunal and in -- in agreement with the federal government, the following decision is made."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The decision refers to the establishment of this expert committee; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was that committee established to help me in any way or for the reasons stipulated here?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the reasons stipulated here, that is correct, certainly. So the committee was not established to give aid to any individual at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let's just have a look now. Let's have a look at another document. Please look at tab 8, because my name is mentioned in it. Yesterday, Mr. Nice showed you this document as well during his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Tab 8. Put the English on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 8.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've found it, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just read out the first sentence, please. What does it say here? "After ..."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "After the trial of Slobodan Milosevic started before the Tribunal in The Hague on the 12th of February, 2002, inter alia also for the crimes allegedly committed by members of the JNA or the army of Yugoslavia in Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Kosovo and Metohija, the Commission of the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia and of the Federal Ministry of Defence for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's no need to read on. Does this pertain to me or is simply a reference being made? You read out the wording there, "crimes allegedly committed by the members of JNA or, rather, the VJ."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my understanding, also on the basis of the request that the Commission for Cooperation sent to us as commanders, namely, that we explain through various documents certain allegations contained in the indictment pertaining to the territories where we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please read out the first line in the second paragraph. It's just a line and a half.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Hague Prosecutor's presentation of numerous inaccurate and biased information as evidence for the Prosecution ..."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the facts that were presented here, you say that there were numerous inaccurate and tendentious information --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... line of questioning that the Chamber's going to indulge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm going to ask you just to make a submission to the Chamber on that -- on that matter. What is your submission as to what this document says? Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document, let me tell you very briefly, shows that the task of the commission is to present truthful facts. That became necessary because, through the media and following what was going on here, they came to the conclusion that untrue facts were being presented. So the commands in charge and the military organs in charge were asked to present the facts as they were, and all of that should be documented as well. Is that a sufficient explanation, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In relation to any particular individual charged by the -- by this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. In relation to any fact which is being presented and which is not true, because the point is to present the actual facts with regard to everything that is being referred to. You see that it was from Mr. Nice that people heard about these allegations, and of course then they ask commanders to say what it was that actually happened then and whether that was correct. And as you could see, none of it was correct. You heard General Delic himself for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. his own area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It has to be said the Prosecution objected, but the accused was reading from a passage of the document. It's the top of page 2, so it was a perfectly valid question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't on the ELMO at the time. Probably that's why the Prosecutor did not see. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look at page 2 and look at paragraph 1. What does it say there: " ... relevant to the authentication of truthfulness and validity of the facts and other issues ..." Is that what is referred to, General?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are those the exact words used in the text?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "To ensure ... the timely provision of all relevant data and suggestions by VJ members, which are relevant to the authentication of truthfulness and validity of the facts ..."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Then in paragraph 2, it says, inter alia, that there should be expertise, under (a), and documents from the archives of Yugoslavia that would refute any allegations made in respect of any current or previous members of the army of Yugoslavia. Any allegations, any accusations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you must allow us to find it in the English. We have to follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 305 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Page --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2(a), Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who are the addressees of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document is addressed to the Chief of Staff -- of General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia, by the commission. The witness can tell you. I don't have to respond to that. It's on page 1. The Commission for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal of the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia. That's what it says. They sent this to the chief of General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia, this particular piece of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In subparagraph 2(a), does it not say that this refutes the incorrect allegations made for any current or former member of the army of Yugoslavia? So what is the task of the commission? What is it that the commission does? Does it collect facts or does it invent things?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of this valid documentation, on the basis of what these persons or, rather, these officers have to state, either as eyewitnesses or direct participants. There should be an answer, and the incorrect allegations made should be refuted in this way for every former or current member of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you now please look at tab 9, which was also shown to you by Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I'm not dealing with all the tabs. I'm only dealing with what Mr. Nice put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice particularly asked you why the commission, because again we are talking about the Commission for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal, why the commission took steps, as he explained it, to make it impossible for persons to make voluntary statements to his investigators. Now, I am asking you to read from page 2, the last paragraph before the section on Providing Legal Aid. Please, is the word "voluntary" written here or is the word "arbitrary" written here? Please read this out to us. Does it say "arbitrarily" or "voluntarily"?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the last paragraph before "Providing Legal Aid"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Measures have been taken to prevent the arbitrary going and giving of statements to The Hague Tribunal office in Belgrade ..."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Since you're not supposed to testify about that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who's translation is this, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is a draft translation provided -- it's a draft translation provided by the office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: By the office?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's an unfortunate error here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'll check and see whether it's an exact translation or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's have the interpreters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can put the B/C/S version on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And ask the interpreters to say whether the correct interpretation is "voluntary" or "arbitrary."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters said "arbitrary" and "arbitrary" is indeed the word that was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want me to read this again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. It's a very bad mistake, Mr. Nice, because it gives a completely different sense to the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will, of course, look into it. All I can say is that the documents arriving when they did, despite the timeous nature of the request, are subject to the best facilities we can make available where resources are not limitless. There it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I hope that this is sufficient. Just one more question in relation to this. Since you are a top general in terms of your training and education, do you know of a single army where arbitrariness is allowed?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. There is anarchy where there is not discipline. There can be no arbitrariness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the very end of this document, as Mr. Nice suggested to you or, rather, he asked you to look at it just before the conclusion, Mr. Nice quoted the last bullet to you. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Cooperation was established and exchange of data and experience with the representatives of the army of Republika Srpska as regards cooperation with The Hague Tribunal until and after their law on cooperation with the Tribunal was passed."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He asked you about established cooperation. And now please go back one page. What is the title of this paragraph where this bullet is contained?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Exchange of Information and Cooperation."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Exchange of Information and Cooperation. And then there are one, two, three, four, five, bullets. Mr. Nice quoted the fifth one.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what does number four say? What does the fourth bullet say? Let us take things in Mr. Nice's order, because he quoted only the last one. What does the fourth one say? Because this has to do with the exchange of information and cooperation, these five bullets.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Daily contact and cooperation have been established with the military-historical institute as well as with the military archives in Belgrade for the purpose of rendering assistance to accused persons from the army and from the Federal Ministry of Defence using the documentation for the preparation of defence before The Hague Tribunal."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So cooperation with military archives in order to have documents provided. Is that the point?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about before that? What was said in the previous bullet, "Regular cooperation and data exchange --"

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Regular cooperation and data exchange with military-judicial organs in Belgrade, Nis, and Podgorica has been established, as well as with --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to read more slowly, for the benefit of the interpreters, and both of you to observe the pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] " ... as well as with other competent courts which have taken over the further conduct of criminal proceedings from the military courts for criminal acts committed in Kosovo and Metohija during the NATO aggression on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the previous page? There are two bullets that pertain to cooperation. What does the first one say? Take it in order, the second one and the first one, because we're doing it in a reverse order anyway.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Contacts have been established, opinions and experiences exchanged with several professors from the Faculty of Law in Belgrade and Novi Sad in order to get information which could increase the level of cooperation with The Hague Tribunal in relation to the VJ and the Federal Ministry of Defence."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does the first bullet say?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Cooperation with state authorities that are in charge and some ministry departments in the Federal Government has been established." In parentheses, it says, "the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of Justice."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what does this section called "Exchange of Information and Cooperation" have to do with? And Mr. Nice quoted only the last bullet to you that had to do with the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has to do with the most important contacts with state organs and institutions that may be of assistance in ensuring the highest quality of work of this commission.

utterances.text: So you heard Mr. Ashdown say that it was a scandal for the international community that they had such poor quality weapons. utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I make it clear, I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't hear that either, and I wonder how it arises from the cross-examination of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it arises --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Probably doesn't. utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that film not a Prosecution exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not part of 76?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think so. We'll hear what the -- if it is, I'll let you know, but it doesn't -- doesn't occur to us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course not. Of course not. Otherwise, it was provided. You saw the date. The 22nd of September, 1998, is the date. Mr. Ashdown was reviewing the weapons of the terrorist organisation, explaining to them what could be used and what could not be used, that they should be careful in using the weapons, and that it is a scandal that they have such poor quality weapons, that Tony Blair had sent him, and so on and so forth. utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... designed to have a certain effect. I would ask the Chamber to confine him to proper re-examination, if he can make any through this -- this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, put your questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, it is true that it is my intention to create a certain effect, because what we see here is a scandal. And it is September 1998. What Paddy Ashdown is doing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I cut you off there, Mr. Milosevic. I have cut you off. Put your question to the witness. And remember, no leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, this is the 22nd of September -- or was it the 28th of September? I'm not quite sure of the date. I mentioned it correctly a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the 28th of September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, the 28th of September, then. Now, what were you able to conclude, seeing this piece of footage?

utterances.text: I don't consider that a proper question in re-examination, or indeed a proper question at all to put to this witness who is not familiar with the video.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody is familiar with the video. Now everybody has become familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, the reports and testimony of Paddy Ashdown, did they relate to that period of time and the descriptions that you saw on the maps when he spoke about certain activities on the part of our army and police in the area of Suva Reka or some other localities in Kosovo and Metohija? utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those are precisely those dates, because Lord Ashdown spoke about the 27th and 28th of September, 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 27th and on the 28th of September, were there any attacks launched by the terrorist KLA organisation on the organs and police in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as that particular region is concerned, that is the Suva Reka area, during that period of time in the area of Jezerce, Budakovo, or along the Sar, Mount Sar Planina, the fifth stage of anti-terrorist operations, or the final stage of anti-terrorist operations was underway because in that area there were about 2.500 terrorists present. utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during that time when Ashdown was in Kosovo, can you roughly tell us how many civilians were killed, civilians and soldiers killed by the KLA, who fell casualty to the KLA? During that time when he was doing this review of weaponry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that doesn't arise. Ask another question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If it doesn't arise from the cross-examination, then -- well, that's correct, actually, directly, but not indirectly. It's not indirectly correct. So I'll just be asking a few more questions, then, relating to Ashdown and this report of his.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point in time you explained to us that one of the maps was a forgery, was false, and that it was done to make it coincide with Paddy Ashdown's report, and Mr. Bonomy cautioned you and said that the first part was a legitimate answer, and as to the second part, you had no grounds to claim that that was done to coincide with the Ashdown report. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't answer that question. It's improper.

utterances.text: The accused has already made it clear that he's using this process of re-examination to great effect. He knows he's acting outside the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're monitoring it, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I would invite the Chamber either to bring it to an end or get Mr. Kay to conclude the re-examination. That's what he's here for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're monitoring the re-examination, Mr. Nice. Mr. Milosevic, next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.text: Even if he were within the unit itself, he could not have concluded that kind of thing. That kind of conclusion would not be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Conclusions, speculation, I don't know what else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will give what weight it considers appropriate to that answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. General, at one point when you were answering Mr. Nice's question you said that the video films were taken from the territory of -- of Yugoslavia, not the territory of Albania, where Ashdown was. On the basis of what have you been saying that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I was responsible for the border, from the border between three areas; Montenegro, Kosovo, and Albania, and all the way down to Peskovi with the border of Macedonia. utterances.text: Mr. Delic, I'm interested to learn what precisely in the video film makes you conclude that it was taken from the territory of Yugoslavia and not Albania where Ashdown was.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I'm saying that I was at that place a countless number of times. A countless number of times I viewed the territory of Metohija. I know exactly what one can see. As for this place where the video was filmed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That doesn't explain it to me. What is it in the film? What's the physical feature or why do you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, the film was taken for a purpose, and then villages are shown; Molic, Brovina, Ponosevac. That someone was on the border viewing Gegaj -- may I just show this, Mr. Robinson, may I show it here so that you can see it clearly as well? Mr. Bonomy yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... in relation to this point, if it's to confirm what you just told me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, precisely. That's what it refers to. Can it be focused a bit? If you look at the area of the village of Batusa, yesterday Mr. Bonomy also noted but on the other picture, see, Batusa has a red line. You see nothing. Molic, again a red line. utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Delic, you wanted to reject these maps out of hand as amateur maps to which no regard should be paid at all. Do you now want to rely on them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to rely on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay, that's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But certainly --

utterances.text: My second question is this: What you didn't see on the film, what none of us saw was the starting point of the filming of this particular one, but we were told that there was a reference to a grid by the use of a GPS system. utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, that doesn't mean anything.

utterances.text: So what are we arguing about? Nothing.

utterances.text: It was a simple answer to the question from the Bench, and I was just checking my memory and Ms. Higgins found it, but the filmer said the border was behind him.

utterances.text: So the place that Lord Ashdown was is one thing, and the visibility from that place is another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's still there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Have you now concluded?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, if what you are claiming is brought into question, would you accept the following possibility: To go to the site itself with the representatives of the other side and to see the grid references contained in all of Lord Ashdown's statements when he testified here - that's the first one - and the second one that is referred to later when he went 300 metres further up? utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At any point in time. Even without a GPS I could go there and I could show them what could be seen from any position. I am ready to go at any time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to the personnel files, Mr. Robinson, I'm not going to put any questions to the general, because this 30th Personnel Centre was explained here, and that just proves that these records were kept there and nothing else. utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, the maps that I drew and that I stand by, although they were done by hand, not by a computer, I guarantee their correctness. I would like them to stay. If the other maps are contained in the evidence, why would the maps that I did personally not be part of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I think that this is perfectly proper, and I ask that this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm quite happy for that to be done.

utterances.text: Is there a reason why it wasn't done?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's not time to do everything --

utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In the passages --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Kay, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've got Exhibit 76 has the clip right --

utterances.text: Yes.

NICE: It lasts about three minutes, and it may be that, providing there's no sound coming over, you'll add the odd comment to it as it's coming, but it will largely speak for itself, I think. "Question: This is you, of course, with binoculars. Now, at what are we looking here? "Answer: You're looking at villages in the area, which I can point out to you later on the map, but roughly the area between Suva Reka and Budakovo, and the villages are being fired -- "Question: Just pausing there. My screen is almost impossible to see. "Answer: Yes, as indeed is -- "Question: -- is the same. It's too light. Perhaps the booth may be able to help. I'm not sure. "Answer: Yes. That's better. "Question: Thank you. So here you'll be able to point out the villages. "Answer: I think they're self-evident there, the ones that are burning. We're looking across the Suva Reka valley and you can see various villages burning, to the left and in the centre of the screen now. We were able to see -- this is one of the houses taken later in the day. We were able to see in amongst those fires the burst of shell-fire. I should point out -- "Question: What are we looking at here? "Answer: This is really the following day. "Question: Let's pause there for a minute. "Answer: I wish perhaps to come to this on the following day. "Question: Thank you. Just pause there. We'll come back --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Should I ask the questions of General Delic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Questioned by Assigned Counsel:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Delic, you saw the video clip there that was an exhibit in the case produced on the 15th of March. Are you able to comment on the location where Lord Ashdown was when he was looking across the valley there in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lord Ashdown said that he was near the village of Pecane. This is the same footage that was already shown to me once here in the courtroom where the location of the village of Pecane is shown. That's the first part of this footage. In this first part, there was also the part that I brought into question when I said that that house in flames cannot be seen from there, and that window too. Now I heard that that was filmed the following day, which is to say that the first part is the 27th and the second part is the 28th. However, on the 27th the lord says that he was in Studencani and that he was at the feature called Grab, above Studencani. This footage was shown to me the first time as if it were near Pecane. The second day you can see that it's raining - that's the 28th - and you can see people who are seeking shelter from the rain. I know that during those days --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, I think Mr. Kay wants you to use your experience of visiting the area so frequently to tell us where Lord Ashdown was from your judgement, having looked at the film. Or have I misunderstood the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Absolutely right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ignore the burning house. Lord Ashdown dealt with that in evidence. Ignore the refugees. Just concentrate on the first 20 seconds where we have a picture of Lord Ashdown with binoculars, we have a picture of green fields, valley, and geography of Kosovo. Are you able to recognise where that precise location was? He described it as being between Suva Reka and Budakovo. Do you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for what you said just now, you probably meant something different. Lord Ashdown certainly could not have been between Suva Reka and Budakovo, because that is in the opposite direction. Lord Ashdown is to the north-west of Suva Reka, somewhere between Studencani and Pecane. Lord Ashdown certainly could not be facing Budakovo, because you see in front of you on this footage a village, and you see part of Suva Reka, which means that he was to the north of Suva Reka, or north-west, rather.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm reading from his evidence before the Trial Chamber, and he described it as roughly in the area between Suva Reka and Budakovo. We saw in the picture smoke coming from locations, villages. Would that area be between Suva Reka and Budakovo?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Then you didn't put your question right to me a few moments ago. What is seen in the front, this smoke, is the area between Suva Reka and Budakovo. In that area there was fighting, and Lord Ashdown is opposite Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell, General Delic, from this whether he's in Serbia or Albania? I'm sorry, yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That issue doesn't arise on this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described earlier today of there being operations conducted by your force in the region between Suva Reka and Budakovo. Was that what we were seeing --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- in the film shot in September by Lord Ashdown?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said today that part of my forces were there fighting, but there were other units of the Pristina Corps there as well. Since my units were on the axis Musutiste-Macitevo, that part could not be seen because it's much too far away. As for the refugees, during our combat activities I found a large number of refugees in the woods, and we kept some of them there until aid and food arrived from Prizren, whereas we sheltered another part of the refugees behind our lines. What I can say for certain is that the refugees were never attacked by the army. And there was a concentration between Macitevo, Vranic, and Bukova Glava, a concentration of refugees in that gorge. There were so many of them that it took us several hours to take them back to their original locations, but first we had to wait for aid from Prizren to arrive; flour, food, medical teams, et cetera, to assist the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, and I think that deals with the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, can you see the still or the clip which appears on the ELMO right now?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you in a position to be able to tell us what is the location where Lord Ashdown was at that time, given your experience?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is north-west of Suva Reka, somewhere close to Pecane village probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To the direction of Pecane?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Pecane should be behind his back, a little further to the north.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So if you could indicate the place in -- using this map. Number 2, somewhere there.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pecane is here, and he was somewhere around this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: From there, can you see Budakovo?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the material that I already worked on, I've pointed this out. It's about 11 kilometres from Budakovo. There are several little townships, mahalas, in Budakovo. Part of Budakovo can be seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next clip is the Suva Reka-Budakovo clip. There's obviously been an intercut of film.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only wanted, Mr. Robinson, to finish things concerning the exhibits now. This film that I've shown, depicting Paddy Ashdown inspecting the weapons of the KLA, I wanted it exhibited. It was filmed on the 28th of September, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't see how it's relevant. It doesn't arise from any questions that I asked. I don't think it's relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we are not with you on that one. It's not linked to anything, it doesn't arise, so we'll not admit that. Mr. Delic, that concludes your testimony. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, yesterday you said that at the end of this examination the issue of exhibits related to 3-D images would be resolved, as well as exhibits --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to deal with all issues now, Mr. Milosevic, related to exhibits. So let me begin. Exhibits related to the testimony of Mr. Delic. And I should say that there are so many that I don't want to take up the time of the Court with the numbering at this stage. That can be done, we'll just deal with those that are admitted and not admitted. I will deal first with a reconsideration of items used during cross-examination and already admitted. First, the photograph and video interview of Nura Nurejeva, the woman interviewed in Exhibit D300, tab 476. These were inadvertently admitted. They had not been tendered for admission by the Prosecution and therefore they are not admitted. Next the statements of Lulzim Kolgjeraj, Mihill Bezhi, and Llesh Lekaj were inadvertently admitted. They had not been tendered for admission by the Prosecution and they are not admitted. General Delic's war diary is marked for identification pending translation. It was not necessary to admit the BBC video clips because they are excerpts from Exhibit 15 and they are not separately admitted. Clips 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 11, 13, and 15 from the programme "Serb Version of the Split" were inadvertently admitted. They had not been tendered for admission by the Prosecution and are not admitted. I turn next to items used during re-examination on the 20th and 21st of September. The topographical manual that accompanied the 3-D pictures of Lord Ashdown's sight lines will be marked for identification pending translation and will form part of the same exhibit. Ian Hendrie's statement is already in evidence as Exhibit 214 and therefore need not be admitted. Similarly, William Walker's 92 bis statement was already admitted as Exhibit 228 and therefore need not be admitted again. The three pictures and the extracts from the book "Atlantic Brigade" are admitted, as well as those parts of Wesley Clark's book referred to. General Delic's order dated September 25, 1998 is admitted. I turn next to exhibits related to the testimony of Mr. Seselj. The transcript of Exhibit 873 is admitted under the same exhibit number as the video clip. The revised transcript for Exhibit 887 provided by the Prosecution is admitted and will replace the current version of the translated transcript. I turn next to the Commission for Cooperation documents produced by the Prosecution. Mr. Milosevic, are you in agreement with these documents being exhibited, or are you in a position to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not oppose the admission of these documents at all, but I would like the document referring to the 30th Personnel Centre admitted as well. I did not deal with the documents that Mr. Nice did not raise. I didn't want to waste time in redirect. I wouldn't have been able to deal with them in redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question was whether you would agree with the admission of those documents among those Commission for Cooperation documents which were not dealt with by Mr. Nice during his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot answer that question because I haven't dealt with these documents at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Then we'll admit only those dealt with by Mr. Nice. That's tab 3, 4, 8, 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. And Mr. Milosevic dealt with tab 1 in his re-exam, so those parts will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Lord Ashdown documents, the three location bundles and the two maps, plus the video of Investigator Kelly, we'll not admit that. Mr. Nice, do you have submissions on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm concerned about the commission documents because although they were put in tab form for the convenience of dealing with them, they were a single -- the reason I put them all to you and made the point that they may yet be incomplete is because they constitute the response of the authorities at the moment to the overall request for commission documents. And the Court will also remember that I urged you to consider the appropriateness, if you're not going to exclude certain documents of Delic, of being able to make written submissions on the totality of these documents to which I confined myself to half an hour's cross-examination, and I would urge you to say with these documents, which are documents that come from the authorities and therefore don't need production by a witness - the fact they came from the authorities doesn't necessarily make them accurate and so on but they -- that's their provenance - I would urge you to admit the documents as a whole because -- and the fact that I only asked questions about a limited number of pages shouldn't compromise that application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is there not an opportunity for you to deal with the remainder of the documents at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there may be. It depends what witnesses come and what priority I give to questioning of witnesses when time is always short. But the reason that the documents are valuable, and you'll remember yesterday that I explained when the accused made an interruption, that yes, the documents contain language of the kind he was identifying today. I accepted that and knew that. But if the documents as a whole need to be reviewed for the effect that they may have on the admissibility of evidence or the weight to be attached to evidence, then it's desirable that they should be admitted as a whole now so that I'm not, as it were, obliged to go through all the other ones with some other Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. witness in order to have them admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the decision's already been made and announced, but even reconsidering it in the light of what you say, this is not the Prosecution case, it's the Defence case, and you cannot just throw a bundle of Prosecution material in and expect it to be freestanding in the context of the Defence case. So I can see no basis for the approach that you're suggesting at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry that Your Honour takes that view, but this is material that arises for the purposes of cross-examination. It would not have been possible, realistically, to, even if we had access to it, to lead it in our part of our case because it wouldn't have been relevant. It arises strictly in relation -- at this stage it arises strictly in relation to the admissibility of Defence exhibits under the rulings that this Court has made, and how can I deal with that -- that it goes to the credibility of the witness, well, that's another matter, but it relates to the admissibility of documents produced by Defence witnesses. It comes as a result of efforts made with the authorities, which were arguably thwarted or in any event nearly thwarted by delay, and in my submission it's material that the Chamber needs to have for the purposes of evaluating the material the witness Delic offers and making the decision whether it should be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, give me an example of a document you say has been presented by the Defence that we need these documents to assess the significance of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's been my argument that those post facto documents, the 2002, 2003 documents, clearly produced with this litigation in mind and on Chamber's own rulings about admissibility of hearsay documents, therefore in contravention of the rules for admissibility. I made that point, I hope, clearly before. And I'll add to it by reminding the Chamber that there is still outstanding the issue of why this witness didn't produce the various contemporaneous documents that were available to him and not available to us despite our RFAs. Why is it that we're relying on statements of his, or the accused through this witness is seeking to rely on statements produced for the commission made in 2002, 2003, not relying on the contemporaneous war diaries and communications of one kind or another? We know as the Prosecution now, and we accept this, which is why I haven't asked for things to be put into evidence, that if I produce material that's been produced for the purpose of this litigation, like, for example, the statement of the woman and her daughter, which explains how it was that she gives a hearsay account that isn't allowed in, I know that I won't be allowed to put that evidence in because the Chamber will turn to me and say that's produced for this litigation, therefore it's not admissible for some reason. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that argument's still available to you but the difference with this witness is that he was there and he is speaking from personal knowledge. So there's that mixed in with the material that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That problem -- that difference may arise for some of his evidence, and his answers are of course before you, but maps which were produced by others than himself and witness statements, or what purport to be witness statements produced by others, in my respectful submission, completely offend the Chamber's own ruling, which we now absolutely understand and with which we willingly comply. So that this material which tells us so much more about the VJ commission, and there may be more to come because there are going to be more RFAs sent to flush out material that should have come the first time and hasn't come. For example, let me just give you an example of -- if I can just get hold of my documents somewhere. I have just a couple -- there was a passage that I didn't take you to in one the other documents, but I must tell you what it says. It's in tab 10, on the second page, under paragraph 5, the tasks of the expert team. Where it sets out the task of the expert team at tab 10, page 2, and it says: "Monitoring and analysing documents and data from the indictments of the Prosecution of The Hague Tribunal against professional VJ members and retired officers, preparation of proposals for defence and rebuttal of allegations in the indictments in the form of professional expert testimonies based on the documentation, preparation of documents regarding the events on the territory," and so on. So there is an expert team, whose composition hasn't yet been provided to us, preparing documents to rebut allegations in the indictments. And that is just another of the matters revealed here that we need further information about, and of course obviously we're going to seek further information (redacted) which you -- I'm sorry, could that be redacted? That's at the moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The two plans referred to. So in my submission, the Chamber is ultimately going to be assisted, both in relation to admissibility of documents through this or other military witnesses, and in relation to assessment of the value of documents by knowing what function the commission served, filter or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All you say may well be true, Mr. Nice, but this is not the way in which to introduce it, in my opinion. If it's not actually used in cross-examination, then it must be another stage and not this one that the Prosecution use to bring this material before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, the liberty of one -- of 30 seconds. I have used the material. I've been provided with what is said to be a complete collection of material. If I put it in as a single tab rather than tabs for ease of handling, I could have said, This is the material I've been provided, this tells me all that is available from the authorities about this commission, please look at these pages. In my submission, that would have been an entirely appropriate course to take, and I would urge the Chamber to admit it all. While I'm on my feet on this topic, if there is a similar application or consideration made in relation to another collection of materials that might have to be dealt with in private session, I would repeat those arguments with the same force, and also urge the Chamber to have in mind the good order and ease of handling of material is much easier if material goes in once and doesn't have to be added to. It goes in once and is there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about marking them -- marking the remainder of the documents for identification until the issue would be resolved at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, a very sensible -- not for me to say that. Yes, it's a proposal that I can understand. The only problem with it is if I'm given leave to argue from the documents about issues of admissibility, I would need to have access to all of them, and I forecast that the accused would likewise want access to the material in toto because, as I heralded and as he explored to a degree this morning, there is language in the material which would suggest, of course, a contrary conclusion to that which I invite, another reason for looking at the material as a whole and seeing what, as a whole, it shows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let me just ask you again so that we can be clear: Are you in agreement with the admission of the Commission for Cooperation documents in their entirety?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, because I haven't had time to read them even. And Mr. Nice hasn't asked questions about these tabs. And let me remind you that when I skip some tabs, even by mistake and don't ask any questions about them, you don't take them into consideration. I don't see why you would take into consideration the documents that Mr. Nice did not cross-examine on. One more thing, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We reaffirm the order made earlier in relation to that. It's only tab 3, 4, 8, 9, which was actually used, and tab 1, which are admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, please, I'm not clear about the fate of this exhibit that I received from Mr. Nice yesterday that relates to the 30th Personnel Centre. It was quoted from and it was on the overhead projector. Mr. Delic read from it. And Mr. Bonomy just said it was related to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll come to that. That's -- he's referring to the letter from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, explaining about that institution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let me just clarify that. It's only those parts in tab 3, 4, 8, 9, and tab 1 which were actually used that are admitted. The 30th Personnel Centre, the letter, the explanation from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, that's admitted. As well as the hand-drawn maps of the witness Mr. Delic. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm looking at your ruling in respect of clips 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 11, 13, and 15 of the programme The Serb Version of the Split.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The position, I believe - Ms. Dicklich is just checking it because we didn't know in advance we'd have to deal with this, they having been admitted - but I think the position is this that I put the clips to the witness and indeed he acknowledged seeing the television programmes concerned, most or all of them, and acknowledged a programme had been made, and I think it may have been inadvertence, it might have been a desire to save time, that I indicated we were going to put that question of applying for them to become exhibits at the end of the evidence of the witness, and that of course, I suppose, would be now unless there was an earlier occasion when we argued about admissibility. And it's our submission that I think he acknowledged seeing these clips at a contemporaneous stage, all bar a couple, but it looks as though His Honour Judge Kwon may have a more detailed and immediate record of what he acknowledged seeing and what he didn't. And it would be our submission that certainly for all those that he acknowledged seeing, then they should be admitted into evidence in accordance with your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm much obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Our records indicate that clips 11 and 15 would meet the requirements for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was not clear to the Chamber whether the Prosecution sought admission of those clips, but once it is clear that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From all those that he acknowledged, and if I can have the opportunity this afternoon --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll admit clips 11 and 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm very much obliged. I don't know if the Court's finished with this issue of exhibits -- sorry, in which case I'll sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I said I've already dealt with the Ashdown documents, the three location bundles, the two maps and the video of Investigator Kelly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we're reconsidering the Ashdown documents, the three location bundles, the two maps and the video of investigator Kelly. We didn't give you an opportunity to make submissions on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'm very grateful. I indicated yesterday that the most I would seek to adduce was the three maps and possibly the video, the video on the basis that the witness has given answers about it, some acknowledging that it shows the potential to see things that can be seen, some otherwise. And it may well be that it is appropriate, and I so invite the Chamber to say that that video should now be admitted. As to the maps, it appears that some shortcomings in the maps were being both asserted and established. For example, I know His Honour Judge Bonomy thought that he could see -- I say thought, explained that he could see something on one of the maps, I think the visibility of Suva Reka, probably, inconsistent with what was shown on the video, and at that stage I was disposed not to press their admission into evidence although I had earlier asserted that they should perhaps be treated sauce for goose, sauce for the gander. That would remain my position, subject only to the use that's been made of the maps this morning by the witness and indeed his answers to Judge Bonomy who sought clarification of whether he was relying on them or seeking not to rely on them. I'm content, of course, for them to be produced as exhibits if they're going to help the Chamber, recognising that they are computer generated documents, and in the same way as I was able to make comments about what I thought were the computer generated documents on which the witness Delic was relying, there it is. So I would apply for the video to be exhibited. I'm content, if it would be helpful, for the maps to be exhibited and can see that it may be appropriate if the Chamber wants to review the answers given about them by the witness in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, on this, on the question of --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness challenged the videotapes and established that they had been filmed from the territory of Yugoslavia, so that they have nothing to do with the positions at which Mr. Ashdown was. Now, if Mr. Nice would like to have that admitted into evidence, that is to say that Ashdown wasn't telling the truth, I have nothing against that, but those videotapes are worthless. And in addition to that, the maps for which Mr. Nice -- which Mr. Nice would like to tender, the witness established that one of them was false, a forgery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are talking about the computer generated maps which were attached to each -- each paper in relation to location 1, 2 and 3.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't state my views about any computer generated maps. You should have asked the witness that while he was here. I'm really not an expert in that type of map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you do not oppose to admitting them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you say that the maps are all right, then I have nothing against them, but I doubt -- very much doubt that, in view of what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit the two maps on Suva Reka, the computer generated maps. We'll not admit the video of Investigator Kelly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The two maps referred to location 2 and 3.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I was not able to conclude from all your quotation -- from everything you said from the exhibits, were the 3-D maps, three dimensional maps admitted with the differences in altitude? Because you just mentioned the topographical data, not the 3-D maps. Were they admitted as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was announced yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admitted those.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, in connection with the question you asked me on the brief closed session we had, 22nd closed session, I would like to say something with respect to that, so I assume we should go back into closed session. Just 20 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is this about? Okay. Let's go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Three points, actually, because I recognise the difficulties that have been caused, developed with the numbering of the production of exhibits, often as a result of good intentioned efforts to speed the process up, but Ms. Dicklich, who has to deal with the consequences of any difficulties or confusion, reminds me that it makes life much easier if, as the more recent practice has been, we deal with them always one at a time as they come to be dealt with, and I would ask that we carry on in that way. Two other points. One, so far as titling of exhibits is concerned, the document of explanation about the 30th Personnel Centre may have been provided by a letter from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, but that should -- in my submission, in the way it's titled in the exhibit list not contain within it the suggestion that it's the Ministry of Foreign Affairs who wrote it. Indeed, I'll return to that issue. It's a anonymous document, undated and unsigned, and I'll deal with a later witness of how it actually came to be prepared. It wasn't provided in the sense of written by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The last point is this: Just a matter of correction dealing with Exhibit 76. Memories can play tricks with us all. When my learned friend Mr. Kay said he was surprised that the exhibit hadn't been dealt with before, and we all worked on that basis, in fact, it had been the subject of cross-examination by me on day 398 at 11.51, and he went through it and then the whole issue turned in his answers to questions about it being a forged video and whatever else. So it had been dealt with there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Nice. Are we in open session? The witness Janicevic should now be brought into Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, you remain subject to the declaration that you made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, please. Examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Janicevic.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just going to remind you that we interrupted your testimony while discussing a series of tabs that related to the question of the goals and features or, rather, the targets of the attacks, where they were targeted, and we went through a series of tabs and stopped off with tab 27, Exhibit 27. So can you find that, please, in the binder containing the exhibits. Tab 27.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I've brought in a certificate regarding the signatures that were illegible. The Judge asked for them. A certificate and confirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon will recall that he asked the witness to identify the signatures done by authorised personnel, signed by authorised personnel on one of the statements, and Mr. Janicevic is going back to that question. So he wants to clear that up before we continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could remind us what the tab number was again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think tab 26.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. At the end of tab 26, you will have -- find three signatures, and you gave the witness authorisation to check that out, because the signatures were illegible. So you asked him who the people were, and he's checked that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please go on. You can put that on the ELMO. Yes, Mr. Janicevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I received this confirmation from the Secretariat of the Interior of Urosevac, which is at present located in Leskovac, and when an investigation was conducted, it was established that Perica Djordjevic and Milan Zivic are the signatories. They are employees of the state security in Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are there not three signatures at the end of tab --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two signatures. It looks as if there are three but in actual fact there are two signatures because one of them is the same person signing twice.
